lesson.title: Sums of Powers: Polynomial Functions and Their Long Run Behavior
lesson.summary: This section defines polynomial functions, introduces degree and leading coefficient, and shows how to factor a cubic completely and use its degree to predict end behavior.
lesson.body:
A polynomial function is any function that can be written as a sum of terms, each consisting of a coefficient multiplied by x raised to a nonnegative whole number power: f(x) = a_n x^n + a_(n-1) x^(n-1) + ... + a_1 x + a_0. The highest power appearing with a nonzero coefficient is the degree of the polynomial, and its coefficient is called the leading coefficient. Linear functions and quadratic functions are the simplest polynomials, of degree 1 and 2 respectively, and everything from here on generalizes the same function notation and evaluation rules already familiar from those simpler cases.

The degree and leading coefficient together completely determine the end behavior of a polynomial, meaning what happens to f(x) as x grows very large in either the positive or negative direction. If the degree is odd and the leading coefficient is positive, the graph falls toward negative infinity on the left and rises toward positive infinity on the right. If the degree is even and the leading coefficient is positive, both ends rise. Flipping the sign of the leading coefficient flips both ends.

Consider p(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - x + 3. This is degree 3 with leading coefficient 1, both positive, so its end behavior is: falls toward negative infinity as x approaches negative infinity, and rises toward positive infinity as x approaches positive infinity. To find where the graph crosses zero, look for rational roots by testing small integers. Trying x = 1: 1 - 3 - 1 + 3 = 0, so x = 1 is a root, and (x - 1) is a factor.

Dividing p(x) by (x-1) gives the quotient x^2 - 2x - 3, so p(x) = (x-1)(x^2-2x-3). This quadratic factors further: x^2 - 2x - 3 = (x-3)(x+1), since -3 times 1 gives -3 and -3 plus 1 gives -2, matching the middle and constant terms. So the complete factorization is p(x) = (x-1)(x-3)(x+1), with roots at x = 1, x = 3, and x = -1. Verify by expanding: (x-1)(x-3) = x^2 - 4x + 3, and (x^2-4x+3)(x+1) = x^3 + x^2 - 4x^2 - 4x + 3x + 3 = x^3 - 3x^2 - x + 3, which matches the original polynomial exactly.

Between consecutive roots, a polynomial's graph cannot cross the x-axis, so it stays entirely above or entirely below it, which means the sign of p(x) can be checked with a single test point in each interval to sketch the graph's overall shape between the three roots at -1, 1, and 3, combined with the falling-then-rising end behavior established from the degree and leading coefficient.
